title: What is DFS (Depth First Search): go as deep as possible first, then backtrack (use recursion or stack); like exploring one path fully before trying another.

s1_definition.oneliner: DFS dives down one path as deep as possible, then backtracks to try the next unexplored branch, using recursion or a stack.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Strategy** – follow one path as far as it goes before backtracking to explore the next branch.
- **Implementation** – naturally expressed with recursion (call stack) or iteratively with an explicit stack.
- **Visited set** – required in graphs to prevent infinite loops on cycles; unnecessary in trees.
- **Applications** – cycle detection, topological sort, connected components, path finding.
- **Complexity** – O(V + E) time, O(V) space for the visited set plus O(h) or O(V) for the stack.
s1_definition.analogy: The fraud team at the National Bank of India traces a suspicious chain of transfers. Starting from Rajesh's account, they follow the money to the next account, then the next, going as deep down one trail as possible. Only when a trail dead-ends do they backtrack to the last branching point and follow a different trail. This is exactly DFS.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
  DFS Traversal: Fraud Trail Tracing

  Transfer Graph:
  Rajesh --> Priya --> Deepak
     |                  (dead end)
     +--> Amit --> Sonal
                   (dead end)

  DFS from Rajesh (recursive):
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ 1. Visit Rajesh                     │
  │ 2. Recurse into Priya               │
  │    3. Recurse into Deepak           │
  │       4. Dead end, backtrack        │
  │    5. Backtrack to Rajesh           │
  │ 6. Recurse into Amit                │
  │    7. Recurse into Sonal            │
  │       8. Dead end, backtrack        │
  │    9. Backtrack to Rajesh           │
  │ 10. Done                            │
  └─────────────────────────────────────┘

  Call Stack at step 4:
  ┌──────────┐
  │ Deepak   │  <-- top (dead end, return)
  │ Priya    │
  │ Rajesh   │  <-- bottom
  └──────────┘

  DFS vs BFS:
  ┌──────────────┐    ┌──────────────┐
  │  DFS (Stack)  │    │  BFS (Queue) │
  │  Goes deep    │    │  Goes wide   │
  │  O(depth)     │    │  O(width)    │
  │  Finds cycles │    │  Shortest    │
  └──────────────┘    └──────────────┘
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Depth-first search follows one path as far as it can go before backtracking to try the next unexplored branch. It is most naturally written with recursion, where the call stack remembers where to backtrack to, or iteratively with an explicit stack. In a graph you need a visited set to prevent infinite loops on cycles; a tree needs no such set.

The key applications are cycle detection (back edge to a node on the active recursion stack), topological sorting (reverse finish order), connected components (each DFS run from an unvisited node discovers one component), and path finding. These make DFS essential for dependency resolution, circuit analysis, and fraud trail tracing.

At the National Bank of India, the fraud team used DFS to trace suspicious transfer chains. Starting from a flagged account, they followed each chain of transfers to its end before trying alternatives. A cycle, where money leaves and returns through intermediaries, was detected as a back edge and flagged as a money-laundering signal.

The senior insight is the memory trade-off: DFS uses space proportional to depth, which is O(log n) for balanced structures but O(n) for deep ones, while BFS uses space proportional to the widest level. For wide graphs DFS is lighter; for deep narrow graphs BFS may be better. Very deep recursion can overflow the call stack, so the iterative version with an explicit stack is safer for production systems.

Remember one sentence: DFS goes deep first using a stack, backtracks on dead ends, and is the basis for cycle detection, topological sort, and connected component discovery.

---

keyPoints: DFS follows one path to its end before backtracking, using recursion or an explicit stack.
A visited set is required in graphs to prevent infinite loops on cycles.
Key applications: cycle detection, topological sort, connected components, path finding.
Time is O(V + E); space is O(V) for visited plus O(depth) for the stack.
DFS memory is proportional to depth; BFS memory is proportional to width.
Back edges (to a node on the active stack) indicate cycles in directed graphs.
